title: Two months of building an ASCII RPG with AI agents: what worked and what failed
author: Basic-Influence2922
selftext:
I'm making Kestrel, a firstperson open world fantasy RPG in ASCII, with my own JavaScript engine with WebGPU. AI agents (mostly Claude Code) write the code. I set the direction, play it and report bugs.
    
    The setup is a small "team": manager, architect, product owner, designer, programmers, tester, writer and a few reviewers. A story gets written, engine work gets a tech note and a code review, and then it is accepted and tested. Since 22 September that has added up to about 8,000 commits and over 2,000 test files.
    
    What worked:
    - Measure the bug first, make fix, and check that the same number moved.
    - New visual looks stay behind a switch until I have seen them on my own screen.
    - For a review, start a fresh reviewer with just the diff and the earlier verdict. Resuming a long conversation cost far more tokens.
    
    What failed:
    - Dots and dither on surfaces cost me 28 hours of back and forth before "no noise, ever" became a written rule.
    - A flicker score kept improving while the same change caused ghost trails for weeks. My eyes caught what the test missed.
    - Stacking a second and third patch on a fix that hadn't moved the measurement.
    
    There is no release date yet. How do you check visual quality when your tests say everything is fine?
